Scenario 4 — Use home equity as a retirement-income bridge
Illustrative planning strategy — not investment, tax or Social Security advice
Robert & Susan • Ages 67 and 66 • Strong investment portfolio • Significant home equity
Instead of selling investments after a significant decline to fund living expenses, they could consider drawing from an available HECM line of credit.
Available HECM proceeds could help cover part of the income gap while one or both spouses delay claiming Social Security.
When markets recover or Social Security begins, they can reassess future HECM draws, portfolio withdrawals and voluntary repayment.
For someone born in 1960 or later, waiting from full retirement age 67 until age 70 increases the monthly retirement benefit to 124% of the full-retirement-age amount.
Sometimes the best time to sell an investment is not immediately after CNBC turns the screen red.
Trade-off: HECM draws increase the loan balance and borrowing costs. Delaying Social Security is not automatically optimal; longevity, taxes, portfolio needs and household circumstances matter.

What happens to the remaining equity?
The reverse mortgage does not automatically take all future equity. Heirs generally deal with the loan payoff when the loan becomes due and payable.

When does the loan become due and payable?

• The last remaining borrower dies.
• The home is sold or title is transferred in a way that triggers repayment.
• The property is no longer the borrower’s principal residence under program rules.
• Borrower fails to meet loan obligations such as taxes, insurance or required property maintenance.
No required monthly P&I does not mean “no obligations.” The borrower must continue to meet HECM and property requirements.
Yes. A HECM can generally be paid off when the homeowner sells, refinances or chooses to repay it.

When it may NOT be the right fit

• The homeowner expects to move again very soon.
• Preserving the maximum possible home equity for heirs is the overriding priority.
• The borrower cannot reliably maintain taxes, insurance or the property.
• A lower-cost alternative solves the same short-term need.
• The homeowner does not understand or is uncomfortable with a growing loan balance.
Good lending means saying “not this time”
The goal is not to make every senior a reverse-mortgage borrower. The goal is to determine whether the tool actually solves the homeowner’s problem.

Five questions to ask before deciding
1. How long do I expect to remain in this home?
2. What cash-flow problem am I trying to solve?
3. How important is preserving home equity for heirs?
4. Can I comfortably keep taxes, insurance and maintenance current?
5. How does this compare with selling, downsizing, a HELOC or a traditional refinance?
